strengths: Learning reusable Sinkhorn initializations from synthetic transport problems is well motivated. Combining supervised potential prediction with adversarial sample generation offers a plausible contribution beyond training on a specific application dataset.

The reported improvements are consistent across four test datasets. Tables 1–2 show average iteration reductions of approximately 16% and 33% at marginal-error thresholds of 1e-3 and 1e-2, respectively. Including marginal feasibility and wall-clock measurements makes the evaluation more informative than transport-cost errors alone.
The manuscript provides network architectures, training pseudocode, hyperparameters, training cost, and a code link. These details provide a useful starting point for reproduction.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish an advance over existing initialization methods. Convergence and runtime experiments compare only against the all-ones initialization, despite discussing Thornton and Cuturi (2022) and Amos et al. (2022). Figure 3 evaluates the alternative training loss through potential MSE; it does not establish which approach produces better Sinkhorn convergence at matched feasibility tolerances.

The central adversarial-training contribution is not isolated experimentally. There is no comparison against a fixed generator or simple random synthetic training distributions under comparable labeling and training budgets. Consequently, the observed gains could come primarily from supervised potential prediction, leaving the benefit of adversarial sample generation unsubstantiated.

Section 3.3 draws a stronger conclusion than Proposition 7 supports. The proposition correctly bounds a dual-objective gap, but this does not establish closeness between unregularized and regularized potentials, even after fixing their additive gauge. Unregularized potentials can be nonunique, and exponentiation can amplify prediction errors. The bound therefore supplies neither potential-error control nor an iteration guarantee; numerically, mnε is approximately 154 in the experiments, making it uninformative at the reported cost scale.

The universality claim exceeds the evidence. All experiments use 784-bin image histograms, one spatial cost matrix, and ε = 0.00025. Even within the stated fixed-dimensional scope, four datasets with added positive mass do not establish reliable performance for arbitrary distribution pairs. Tests on concentrated or otherwise difficult marginals and across regularization strengths would strengthen this claim, particularly because flexibility in ε motivates learning unregularized potentials.

The standalone barycenter application is insufficiently validated. Figure 7 presents four qualitative outputs without reference barycenters, objective errors, or runtime comparisons. The error-cancellation argument assumes unbiased prediction errors without establishing that assumption; unbiased objective estimates at a fixed measure would also not establish accurate gradients or minimizers.

Material evaluation details remain unspecified in the manuscript, including test-pair counts and sampling, the number of independent training runs, how confidence intervals were constructed, and the positivity offset used for test distributions. Numerical precision, stabilization, and the timing breakdown for prediction and the C-transform also need clarification to assess reproducibility and the claim of negligible initialization overhead.
